evidence_quotes.quote: The aim of this scoping review was to summarise the available evidence for the effectiveness of behaviour change interventions in promoting better household connectivity to sewers.
Most interventions to increase connectivity focused on addressing financial, social, and legal barriers
Thus, we aim to understand the effectiveness of behaviour change interventions in increasing the uptake of sewer connections.
The majority (9 out of 11) of the studies were in professional or technical project reports, with all being overviews of implemented projects.
We followed the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR) checklist to conduct the review [26].

Eleven articles met the eligibility criteria and were included in the review. Findings indicate that changes in rates of connection were associated with interventions that included a blend of indirect financial subsidy in the form of a free connection and community-engagement activities.

criterion_notes.c1: Examines household off-site sanitation service access, specifically household connectivity to sewerage networks in urban and rural communities.
criterion_notes.c2: Fails both the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading and the plain wording of Criterion 2 (plain_criterion2_decision = exclude; narrow decision = exclude). Under the plain wording, the scoping review explicitly restricts its research question and search strategy to behaviour change interventions to promote sewer uptake (promotional campaigns, educational trainings/workshops/kits, community engagement and project-delivered free connections), explicitly contrasting its focus with studies of legal barriers in the abstract; although project-level connection subsidies (such as Output-Based Aid or government-funded free connections) and participatory condominial construction involve institutional programme delivery, the review does not examine a legal, administrative, institutional, regulatory or governance factor as its analytical exposure. Under the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading, the study clearly fails because the clarification expressly excludes generic project delivery, behavioural promotion and unanalysed macro-governance background: 9 of 11 included items are project implementation reports evaluating behavioural promotion and free physical connection delivery, while mandatory connection laws (in Sao Paulo, Tamil Nadu and Salvador) appear only as unanalysed background notes in Table 2 without any evaluation of statutory mandates, enforcement, eligibility screening, administrative burden, tenure/documentation rules or tariff/cost-recovery rules.
criterion_notes.c3: Contains a systematic empirical synthesis: a PRISMA-ScR scoping review searching four bibliographic databases plus grey literature (10,017 records identified, 33 full texts screened, 11 project case studies/reports included), with dual screening, critical appraisal using an adapted JBI checklist and synthesis of empirical baseline-to-endline sewer connection outcomes.
criterion_notes.c4: Reports household sewer connection uptake (numbers and percentages of targeted households connected to the sewer network from baseline to endline across included projects).
criterion_notes.c5: Population and unit of analysis (targeted households across 11 urban and rural sewer projects), exposure (behaviour change intervention packages combining free connections, promotion, education and community engagement), outcome (household sewer connection rate) and study design (PRISMA-ScR scoping review) are all clearly identifiable.
criterion_notes.c6: Full text is published in English.

study_design: Scoping review (PRISMA-ScR) synthesizing 11 implemented project case studies and technical reports
country: Multi-country (Brazil, Colombia, Ecuador, Bolivia, Morocco, Kenya, India and Pakistan)
population_and_sample: Targeted urban (10 studies) and rural (1 study) household populations across 11 included sewer project case studies/reports (selected from 10,017 records and 33 full-text articles); unit of analysis in the synthesis is the implemented project / targeted household cohort
exposure: Behaviour change interventions to promote sewer connectivity, grouped into indirect subsidies (project-provided free household sewer connections), promotional activities (door-to-door and awareness campaigns), educational interventions (trainings, workshops and educational kits) and community engagement
outcome: Change in the number and percentage of targeted households connected to the sewer network after intervention implementation (baseline to endline connection rates)
rationale: Exclude under E03 (Wrong exposure). Although this PRISMA-ScR scoping review examines household sewer connection uptake (c1=yes, c3=yes, c4=yes, c5=yes, c6=yes), its synthesized exposure is behaviour change promotion and project-delivered free connections (promotional campaigns, hygiene/environmental education, community mobilisation and upfront free connection installation in implemented projects) rather than a rule-type legal, administrative, institutional, regulatory or governance mechanism governing service access (c2=no). Mandatory connection laws in three settings are noted only as unanalysed background in Table 2 and are not evaluated.
